2028 Ford Mustang Cobra Sound Teaser Indicates FPC V8 Engine, Manual Transmission, Cobra R Variant
21 photos
Photo: Ford / edited
The C8-generation Corvette Z06 is the only American series-production model to feature a naturally aspirated flat-plane V8 as of this writing. Come 2027 for model year 2028, the Ford Motor Company will also gift us a free-breathing V8 with a flat-plane crankshaft. Based on FoMoCo's recently posted teaser clip, the Voodoo in the S550-generation Mustang Shelby GT350 is coming back with a vengeance.
Said teaser clip shows the Cobra name, a moniker that first appeared on a Ford-affiliated vehicle in the 1960s with the debut of the Shelby Cobra. A few years after that, the Cobra name was applied to the 428 Cobra Jet V8-powered Fairlane Cobra and Torino Cobra. Speaking of which, the USPTO database shows Ford as the legal entity that owns the Cobra wordmark in the United States market.
Previously believed to be christened Dark Horse Boss after a different wordmark owned by the Dearborn-based automaker, the next iteration of the Cobra is certain to feature a manual option. You can hear that in the teaser clip, where the distinct pause during upshifts indicates a third pedal rather than a torque converter or a dual-clutch arrangement.
Rumored to come exclusively as a fastback, the 2028 model year Cobra may not even be offered with a two-pedal option. The 10R that Ford developed as part of a joint venture with General Motors never saw a high-revving application. For reference, the dual-throttle-body Coyote engine of the GT and Dark Horse doesn't go higher than 7,500 revolutions per minute.
The manual-only Shelby GT350, meanwhile, shoots to 8,250 revolutions per minute. Said maximum engine speed applies to the GT350R as well. Toward the end of the teaser video, the R in COBRA with all caps is highlighted in blue.
It's also stylized differently from the other letters, and this detail alone is enough for me to get all giddy about a potential Cobra R variant. In a similar fashion to the GT350R from a decade ago, it should come with less weight, better aero, and track-focused chassis tuning.
Photo: Ford The old R offered carbon-fiber wheels, stickier Michelin rubber shoes, a larger front splitter, a carbon-fiber rear wing, and MagneRide damping. To keep it light, Ford removed the rear seats and something else. Indeed, the GT350R did not feature standard air con, floor mats, a tire inflator and sealant kit, or an audio system. The Electronics Package restored much of the deleted equipment, including the floor mats.
Hearsay suggests a wider body than you get with the Coyote-powered Dark Horse, bringing the Cobra a little closer to the supercharged Dark Horse SC styling-wise. While Dark Horse SC-rivaling output figures are completely out of the question, the flat-plane V8 of the Cobra should easily surpass the 500 horsepower of the Dark Horse's engine.
Ford claims the S550-generation Shelby GT350 is good for 526 horsepower at 7,500 revolutions per minute and 429 pound-feet (582 Newton-meters) at 4,750 revolutions per minute. By comparison, the Dark Horse makes 500 horsepower at 7,250 revolutions per minute and 418 pound-feet (567 Newton-meters) at 4,900 when you give it 93-octane premium unleaded.
As noted earlier, the only flat-plane naturally aspirated V8 available in a mass-market American model today is the LT6 of the Corvette Z06. The Detroit-based automaker used Ferrari's architecture as inspiration for this bad boy, whose 5.5 liters of displacement makes it the largest NA FPC V8 to ever grace a series-production model.
Priced from $121,800 for model year 2027, the mid-engine supercar from Kentucky revs slightly higher, with Chevrolet advertising 8,600 revolutions per minute. In optimal conditions, the Voodoo's only American rival develops 670 ponies at 8,400 revolutions per minute and 460 pound-feet (624 Newton-meters) at 6,300 revolutions per minute.
